title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days, once you have worked through the topics and taken your mocks. The aim now is to sharpen what you know, not to learn new material. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days take longer.
how_it_works: Short reviews spread over several days hold up better than one long session the night before.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with today's plan. Doubling up turns review into cramming.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the time of day your exam starts, to test your pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Take a full timed mock in one sitting at your exam's start time, with your phone away and no notes.
Practice the pace: about 96 seconds a question. Past 2 minutes on one question, choose your best answer, flag it and move on.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: One mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. A single score can swing from day to day.

days.title: Learn from every miss
days.goal: Trace each mock miss back to the thinking slip behind it. Stop after about 90 minutes, even if some are left.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from yesterday's mock, starting with Domains 4 and 5.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list three Domain 4 and three Domain 5 points. Then open the lists and check.
Read the principles on what comes first when something goes wrong; they pair with Domains 4 and 5.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: Your biggest gap
days.goal: Work on the domain where your readiness is furthest behind its weight on the exam.

tasks.text: Before opening your focus domain's list, write down what you remember. Then check for gaps.
Answer a short set in that domain, rating how sure you are before you check each answer.
Review first the answers you felt sure of but got wrong. Those are the ones to fix.
For a topic you missed more than once, read its note, then close it and explain the idea in two sentences.
Read the principles about your role as the IS auditor.

days.remember: Weight matters: Domains 4 and 5 together are just over half the exam.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your exam pace sharp with one timed mini mock, and refresh the IS auditor's method behind every domain.

tasks.text: Take a timed mini mock in one sitting. Watch the pace checks more than the score.
From memory, list three Domain 1 and three Domain 2 points. Then open the lists and check.
Without looking, say what makes evidence stronger or weaker, then check the note.
Read the principles on how you know something is true.
Read the principles on what matters most: business goals and risk.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Read like the exam
days.goal: Sharpen how you read each question, work on your second gap and cover the smallest domain.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Domain 3 points. Then open the list and check.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short set in your second-weakest domain. Name the priority word before you read the options.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: Several options are often true. The priority word decides which one wins.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Recall everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details, so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each domain, recall two points before you open its list. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Read the principles on which fix actually works.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your booking, ID and route, or run the online system check again.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: answer up to 10 mistake journal questions, then stop. A miss today is a reminder, not a warning.
Read the reminder for the slip you make most often.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your booking is confirmed, and you have checked the ID and exam-day rules in ISACA's Exam Candidate Guide.
Online: the system check is done and your desk is clear. Test center: your route and travel time are planned.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your pace plan: about 96 seconds a question, with a checkpoint each hour.
Arrive at least 30 minutes early, or start online check-in when it opens.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, flag the question and come back to it.

points.text: Roles: the audit committee approves the audit charter and receives audit results; management owns the controls and the corrective actions; the IS auditor assesses, reports and follows up.

Preventive controls stop a problem, detective controls find it and corrective controls fix it; prefer preventive where practical. IT general controls (ITGCs) underpin application controls, so they are tested first.
Audit risk combines inherent, control and detection risk. The IS auditor can only adjust detection risk, through more or better testing.

Compliance tests check that a control works (attribute sampling); substantive tests check the data itself (variable sampling); discovery sampling looks for at least one case, such as fraud. Strong controls allow less substantive testing.
Evidence is stronger when it is independent, obtained directly by the IS auditor and documented. Treat that as a guide, not a strict ranking. Inquiry alone is never enough.
Continuous auditing belongs to the audit function; continuous monitoring belongs to management. Control self-assessment (CSA) adds to audit work but never replaces it.

Suspected fraud: make sure evidence is preserved and report above anyone who may be involved, such as to the audit committee. Recommend investigation by qualified specialists; never alert the suspect or lead the investigation.
The board governs: it sets direction and risk appetite and provides oversight. Management runs IT within that direction. Governance answers usually come before management answers.
Three lines: management owns and manages risk; risk and compliance functions support, monitor and challenge; internal audit gives independent assurance.
Policy says what and why and is approved by the board or senior management; standards set mandatory specifics; procedures give the steps; guidelines advise.
Risk responses are accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid. The risk owner chooses within the risk appetite the board sets; the IS auditor never accepts risk.

Segregation of duties splits incompatible tasks, such as requesting, approving, recording and holding assets, so no one person can both cause and hide an error. Where a small team can't separate them, add an independent review.
Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability. Contracts need service levels and a right to audit, and the organization still needs assurance.
The data owner, in the business, classifies data and approves access; the data custodian, usually IT, runs the controls the owner decides.

domains.name: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation

points.text: The business case justifies the project and is revisited at each phase gate. If the benefits no longer hold, the project should be reconsidered.

Control and security requirements belong in requirements and design, where they cost least. The IS auditor advises on them but does not design controls or sign off; those decisions stay with management.
Test levels run unit, integration, system, then user acceptance testing (UAT). Business users and the process owner sign off UAT, not the developers.
Keep development, test and production apart. Under segregation of duties, developers do not move their own code to production; changes are approved and tested first.
Changeover (cutover): parallel is safest but costliest, abrupt (direct) changeover is riskiest, and phased and pilot sit between. Data conversion needs reconciled record counts and control totals.
Source code escrow protects the buyer if a vendor fails, but only with clear release triggers and deposits that are kept current and verified.
The post-implementation review comes after the system has settled. It compares results with the business case and checks that controls work.

domains.name: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience

points.text: The business impact analysis (BIA) comes first: it finds critical processes and sets recovery priorities and targets. The BCP keeps the business running; the DRP, one part of it, restores IT.

RPO is how much data you can afford to lose and drives backup frequency; RTO is how fast service must return and drives the recovery site. RTO must sit inside the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD). Tighter targets cost more.
Recovery sites: hot is ready within hours, warm needs setup, cold is space and power only. Reciprocal agreements are hard to enforce.
Full, incremental (changes since the last backup) and differential (changes since the last full) backups trade backup time against restore time. Keep a copy offsite and test restores.
Recovery tests build up from checklist and walk-through to simulation, parallel and full interruption, which carries the most risk.
Incident management restores service quickly; problem management finds and removes the root cause.
Every change needs approval, testing and a back-out plan. Emergency changes are still documented and approved afterward.

Least privilege and need to know: the data owner approves access, reviews it regularly and has it removed promptly when people leave. Staff who change roles keep old access unless reviews catch it (privilege creep).
Multi-factor authentication needs factors of different types: something you know, have or are. A password plus a security question is still one factor.

Encryption protects confidentiality; hashing shows integrity; a digital signature, made with the sender's private key, shows integrity, origin and non-repudiation. Encrypt with the recipient's public key to keep a message secret.
In a public key infrastructure (PKI), the certificate authority (CA) signs certificates that bind a public key to an identity. Revoked certificates are listed on a certificate revocation list (CRL).
An intrusion detection system (IDS) detects and alerts; an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and blocks. A firewall enforces rules between network zones.
Incident response runs prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, then lessons learned. Preserve evidence and its chain of custody throughout.

In the cloud, the provider secures what it runs and the customer secures its data, identities and settings; the split depends on the service model. Accountability for the data stays with the customer.

principles.intro: The 20 mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. What must happen before anything else? Usually understanding or assessing comes before acting; if harm is spreading right now, containing it comes first.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what does everything else depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the strongest overall: within your role, fixing the cause and covering the most.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which would I defend to the audit committee?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST effective, MOST important or MOST reliable. Judge the options on that quality only.
The core purpose or main reason, not a side benefit or a nice extra.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For risk or concern, the worst exposure with the widest business effect; for assurance or benefit, the strongest.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and for the whole business?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What is most probable given the facts, even if another outcome would be worse.
Flip the logic. Three options do the job; find the one that does it worst or not at all.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is being asked: an action, a risk, a purpose or a piece of evidence.

answering_routine.title: Find the priority word
answering_routine.text: Spot FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Check your role and the moment
answering_routine.text: You are the IS auditor unless told otherwise. Is this before, during or after the event? Note limiting facts such as “already”, “new” or “small organization”.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options with the wrong role, the wrong order, an absolute word, an action outside scope or a fix for a symptom.

answering_routine.title: Decide between the final two
answering_routine.text: Apply the priority word, then prefer the option that comes earlier, covers more, fixes the cause and fits your role.

pace: 240 minutes for 150 questions is 96 seconds each. Aiming for about 90 leaves time to review flagged questions.
Checkpoints: around question 40 at 1 hour, 80 at 2 hours and 120 at 3 hours.
Past 2 minutes on one question, choose your best answer, flag it and move on. Never leave a question blank.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as a fact or a priority word you missed the first time.
